responses.mission_1.search: On the open map, BFS and A* both found a path of 13.5 meters. With that being said, BFS expanded 928 nodes, while A* expended only 700 nodes meaning that A* examined fewer cells. In my BFS code, I used a FIFO queue, which explores cells in the order they were added. In A*, I used a priority queue and the heuristic to prioritize cells with the lower estimated total cost. This is what helped A* find the shorts path while having to explore fewer cells.
responses.mission_1.failure: On the constrained map, BFS found a path of 24.5 meters, while DFS found a longer path of 50 meters. This happened because my DFS implementation uses a stack and explores one path deeply before trying other paths, so it doesn't guarantee the shortest path. IDDFS reached the resource limit after 250,001 expansions because it repeatedly searches with increasing depth limits. On the unreachable map, all four algorithms returned no_path which means that they finished searching and didn't find any possible route. This is different from resource_limit which means that the search stopped because it ran out of time or expansions. It doesn't mean that the path doesn't exist. I used AI to help me write part of the code for IDDFS and A*. I worked thought the logic myself, wrote parts of the algorithms myself, and checked my implementations using the provided tests and evaluation results.
responses.mission_2.prediction: I predict that A* with finish sooner than DFS on the constrained map. In Mission 1, A* found a path of 24.5 meters, while DFS found a much longer path of 50 meters. Since A* uses a heuristic to find a shorter path, I think the robot will need to travel less distance and will get to the goal faster.
responses.mission_2.performance: My prediction was supported because A* performed better than DFS on the constrained map. A* was able to reach the goal in 90.0 seconds and traveled 23.91 meters, while DFS failed after 144.6 seconds and traveled 31.47 meters. Looking at the graphs, we can see that DFS planned a route with a lot of unnecessary turns, and the robot rounded several of the sharp turns, and the execution eventually failed with Nav2 controller error 104. For example, at checkpoint 723, the robot was making one of these turns, and its estimated path error was 0.09 meters. This shows that finding a path doesn't always mean that the robot will be able to successfully reach its goal.
responses.mission_2.choice: Looking at the results, I would choose Nav2 as my delivery planner because it succeeded on both maps and had the fastest execution times among the successful planners. On the open map, it reached the goal in 35.6 seconds, while on the constrained map, it reached the goal in 73.4 seconds. In comparison, A* was also successful on both maps, but it took 46.4 seconds on the open map and 90.0 seconds on the constrained map. Nav 2 also traveled shorter distances, 10.10 meters on the open map and 20.60 meters on the constrained map, compared to A* with 13.17 and 23.91 meters. I think the most important advantage for a delivery robot is being able to reach its destination successfully and quickly, which is why I would go with Nav 2.
responses.mission_3.prediction: I tested the constrained map and first changed the repulsion strength for social_2 from 1.30 to 0.90, while keeping everything else unchanged. The robot still got stuck, but the failure changed from oscillation to an obstacle local minimum. So I then decided to reduce the influence distance from 1.50m to 1.00m, keeping the repulsion strength at 0.90 and the refinement step at 0.08m. After this change, the robot was finally able to find a complete path. The new path stayed close to the original one, with only small changes near the person. This shows that stronger repulsion and a larger influence distance don' t always improve the path since they can potentially cause our robot to get stuck.
responses.mission_3.comparison:
For A*, social_2 had the largest minimum person clearance at 0.759 meters, compared to 0.706 meters for the baseline. It also reduced the time spent inside personal space from 1.8 seconds to 0 seconds. The execution time went down a little from 46.4 to 46.1 seconds, while the distance barely changed from 13.13 to 13.14.

For RRT, the baseline had the largest minimum clearance at 1.728 meters, compared to 1.722 meters for social_1 and 1.699 meters for social_2. All three spent 0 seconds inside personal space. The baseline was also the fastest at 43.3 seconds, compared to 44.6 seconds for social_2. This shows that stronger repulsion doesn't always make the route better, especially when the robot already stays far away from the person.
responses.mission_3.recommendation: I would choose RRT with the baseline setting because it successfully reached the goal, had the largest minimum person clearance of 1.728 meters, and finished in 43.3 seconds. In comparison, A* with social_2 had a clearance of 0.759 meters and took 46.1 seconds . So RRT was both faster and stayed farther away from the person. With that being said, these trials only tested a person standing still. They can't tell us how the our robot would react if someone suddenly walked in front of it or changed direction. We would need to test it with moving people to see how well it performs in those situations.
responses.final.synthesis:
Across all three missions, I learned that finding a path is only one part of successful robot navigation. In Mission 1, we compared different search algorithms and saw how some were better at finding shorter paths or searching more efficiently than others. 

With that being said, Mission 2 showed us that even if a robot is able to find a path, it doesn't always mean it can successfully follow it. For example, on the constrained map, A* reached the goal in 90.0 seconds, while DFS failed after 144.6 seconds because of a controller error. DFS had a lot of unnecessary turns and therefore, the route was a lot harder to follow.

Mission 3 showed how important it is to consider people when planning routes. For example, A* with social_2 increased the minimum distance from the person from 0.706 to 0.759 meters without adding a lot of time. However, RRT already stayed far away from the person and adding repulsion didn't improve its results. Overall, I think a good route should be efficient, easy for the robot to follow, and safe for people around it. We also need to keep in mind that the robot's position and distance measurements are estimates meaning they might not be fully accurate.
responses.final.course_reflection: What stood out to me the most about this lab was seeing how differently the robot performed depending on the planner we used. I found it especially interesting that even though DFS was able to find a path, the robot still failed to reach its goal because the path was hard to follow. I didn't see this coming at all. I also liked the last mission because it made me think about how a robot needs to consider the people around it, not just obstacles. So sometimes it might be a better choice to take a longer route if it gives people more personal space.
